Roger Wayne Marshall (born August 9, 1960) is an American politician and physician serving as the junior United States senator from Kansas since 2021. representative for Kansas's 1st congressional district from 2017 until 2021.
Marshall practiced medicine as an obstetrician for more than 25 years before being elected to Congress in 2016. He ran for reelection in 2026, but lost to Democratic nominee Adam Hamilton.
Early life and education

Marshall was born in El Dorado, Kansas, in the fifth generation of a farming family. Both of his grandfathers owned farms on which he worked as a child, his father was a police chief, and his mother an office clerk.

His generation was the first to go to college, and he attended Butler Community College before studying at Kansas State University, where he received a Bachelor of Science in biochemistry and was a member of the Beta Theta Pi fraternity.
Marshall received his Doctor of Medicine from the University of Kansas. He completed a residency in obstetrics and gynecology at Bayfront Medical Center in St.
Physician career

In 1998, Marshall and eight other doctors opened Great Bend Regional Medical Center in Great Bend, Kansas, where he worked as an obstetrician-gynecologist. From 1998 to 2012 he was owner and 2013 to 2019 co-owner of Heartland Regional OBGYN.

According to a September 2026 New York Times report, Marshall charged patients an 18% annual interest rate on medical debt, and he and Heartland Regional sued more than 700 patients for bills ranging from $101 to thousands of dollars.
Reportedly at the request of Marshall's lawyers, at least 81 defendants were arrested for not appearing in court.
Marshall responded by saying his medical firm only used "common business practices", calling the report a "hit job".

His spokesperson said he treated all patients regardless of ability to pay, that he welcomed Medicaid patients, that his firm used standard billing and collection procedures, and that his firm provided millions of dollars in free medical care.

Marshall served as vice president of the Farmers Bank and Trust, and was a district governor of Rotary International. He also served seven years in the United States Army Reserve, where he trained a mobile hospital support unit, reaching the rank of captain.
U.S. House of Representatives
2016 campaign
Marshall ran against incumbent Tim Huelskamp in the Republican Party primary election for Kansas's 1st congressional district in the United States House of Representatives.

Marshall had the support of many of Kansas's agricultural groups, who were angry that Huelskamp lost his seat on the House Agriculture Committee, the first time in a century that no Kansan was on that panel.

Marshall was endorsed by the United States Chamber of Commerce, the Kansas Livestock Association, the National Association of Wheat Growers, and the Kansas Farm Bureau, an affiliate of the American Farm Bureau Federation.

During the primary, Huelskamp criticized Marshall over a 2008 confrontation with a neighbor during a land dispute. The neighbor accused Marshall in a 911 call of trying to run him over with his truck. The Barton County Sheriff's Office filed a complaint charging Marshall with battery and reckless driving.
Prosecutor Carey Fleske dropped the battery charge as part of plea negotiations, and Marshall pleaded no contest to reckless driving.

On Christmas Eve, Fleske (whose father was Marshall's business partner and neighbor) obtained a court order from a different judge who was available, replacing the conviction with a minor traffic infraction on the basis that the earlier documents had been typed up incorrectly.
On August 2, Marshall defeated Huelskamp in the Republican primary, 56% to 44%. No Democrat filed to run in the heavily Republican district.
Tenure

Marshall was sworn into office by House Speaker Paul Ryan on January 3, 2017. As a congressman, Marshall regained a seat for his district on the House Agriculture Committee after a three-year lapse, which positioned him to protect crop insurance.
The 2018 Farm Bill then did so, while also protecting the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP).
On October 23, 2019, Marshall was part of a group of 15, 30 House Republicans, led by Representative Matt Gaetz, who intruded upon that day's confidential hearing of the House Intelligence Committee.

The Republican and Democratic committee members were meeting in a Sensitive Compartmented Information Facility (SCIF) to hear testimony from Deputy Assistant Secretary of Defense Laura Cooper in connection with the impeachment inquiry against Donald Trump. Marshall was one of a group of Republicans that followed Gaetz to the hearing room.
U.S. Senate

In September 2019, Marshall announced he would give up his House seat to run for the Senate seat being vacated by four-term incumbent Pat Roberts. In the Republican primary election, Marshall faced Kris Kobach, a polarizing ex-Kansas Secretary of State and Donald Trump ally known for his far-right views.

Senate Republican leaders, fearing that Kobach's nomination would endanger their majority in the Senate, urged Trump to endorse Marshall, Trump did not. Chamber of Commerce, the Kansas Farm Bureau and several anti-abortion organizations supported Marshall. 3 million unique voter contacts via text and robocalls in the week before the election.
3% of the vote, although the second-place finisher (Kobach) and third-place finisher (Kansas City based plumber Bob Hamilton) combined for a higher total.

Marshall won all but one county west of Emporia. In Sedgwick County, which contains Wichita, he beat Kobach 47% to 26%. He lost by a majority in Wyandotte County, which contains Kansas City, and by pluralities in most counties in eastern Kansas.

In the general election, Marshall defeated Democratic State Senator Barbara Bollier 53% to 42%, with the Libertarian Jason Buckley receiving 5%. He succeeded Roberts, who represented the 1st from 1981 to 1997, Kansas's senior senator, Jerry Moran, represented the district from 1997 to 2011.
Marshall announced his candidacy for reelection in July 2025. He faced Democratic nominee Adam Hamilton in the general election. Senate seat from Kansas in 94 years.
Tenure

In October 2021, Business Insider reported that Marshall had violated the Stop Trading on Congressional Knowledge (STOCK) Act of 2012, a federal transparency and conflict-of-interest law, by disclosing up to 17 months late stock purchases made by one of his dependent children.

Political positions
Marshall voted in line with President Trump's positions 98% of the time.

On January 6, 2021, Marshall was a leading advocate of Trump's efforts to overturn his election loss, and was one of the five senators who objected to both the certification of Arizona's and Pennsylvania's electoral votes.
2021 attempt to overturn the 2020 presidential election results

Marshall disputed the results of the 2020 presidential election, claiming that in "several states" "governors, secretaries of states and activist courts" usurped legislatures to create voting rules. Therefore, he announced that he would oppose the January 6, 2021, certification of the Electoral College count.
Marshall was participating in the certification of the Electoral College count when Trump supporters stormed the United States Capitol.

After the Capitol was secure, Marshall joined the Senate to continue the vote on the certification. Marshall supported the objections to Arizona's and Pennsylvania's electoral votes. The Senate rejected these objections by 93, 6 and 92-7 respectively.
" Following the vote on certification, Marshall acknowledged that Joe Biden would be president and urged a peaceful transition of power.

As a result of his refusal to certify the count, the Kansas Democratic Party called for his expulsion from Congress for failure to "execute oath of office to support and defend the United States Constitution".
The McPherson Sentinel editorial board wrote that Marshall "should be ashamed" of his decision to support false claims of voter fraud and trying to overturn the election.
On May 28, 2021, Marshall voted against creating an independent commission to investigate the 2021 United States Capitol attack.
Abortion
Marshall opposes abortion, including in cases of rape and incest. In 2020, he called for overturning Roe v. Supreme Court decision that ruled abortion bans unconstitutional.
